Deterministic projection of ORT's biased batch=2, q_seq=3, kv_seq=5, num_heads=2, head_size=40 cross-attention topology.
Covers ORT's batch=1, q_seq=2, kv_seq=3, num_heads=2, head_size=16 biased cross-attention shape.
ORT cross-attention with batch 1, two query rows, three key/value rows, two heads of width 16, and no bias.
Small ORT cross-attention topology with head_size=8 and no bias.
Projects ORT's packed self-attention topology into separate Q/K/V inputs and enables the local unidirectional path.
A compact decode with eight heads, head size 128, and a long KV sequence exercises split-K attention.
A float16 prefill with head size 128 exercises the q32 broadcast route with subgroups and the shared-memory q32 route without them.
Upper-left causal masking with two queries and four keys. The second query averages only the first two values, producing exactly 1.5.

A 65,537-row query exceeds the flash-path cap and exercises the scalar fallback's folded dispatch. The x dimension is capped at 65,535, so a grid-stride iteration handles the final two distinct rows; two keys keep expected-value evaluation compact.
A compact sequence-64, 16-head prefill exercises the clustered route and its no-subgroups fallback.
A 32-token sequence with 8 heads and head width 128, drawn from FLUX.2's joint attention, checks attention output at a compact scale.
A compact fused-bias case exercises the boundary of 32 four-wide head segments across 32 lanes.
A 31-token query against a 511-token key/value context, with 8 heads and head width 64, checks attention for a short query length paired with a context length one below 512.
A 2-token query against a 2048-token key/value cache with 4 heads and head width 32 checks short-query, long-context attention output.
Decode attention with head dimension 32 and long context checks output on subgroup and portable tiers.
Head size 6 exercises the key-parallel fallback with multiple keys per lane and a compact expected output.
Float16 head size 6 exercises the key-parallel fallback. Values remain near one while queries and keys stay small, keeping scale errors observable.
Sixteen queries over eight heads and 2,048 keys check attention normalization with a short query sequence.
A 512-token float32 prefill with one head and head width 128 checks QK scores, softmax normalization and the weighted-value combination.
Float16 attention with 1024 queries and keys, 4 heads of width 64, an explicit scale of 0.125 and no bias; scores are accumulated in float32.
Float16 head size 80 and a large score matrix check partial head tiles and guarded reads.
A 128-wide attention head with Q, K, and V bias checks their distinct effects: K bias adds one constant to every logit in a query row and cancels under softmax.
Head size 320 exercises the portable route used by wide vision and multimodal attention blocks.

A six-head f32 decode geometry where head size 64 supplies only 16 vec4 dot products to a 32-lane subgroup. The case exercises the portable split-K route instead of an underfilled cooperative QK subgroup.
A 1500-query, 1500-key, two-head attention shape (head width 64) exercises the sequence tail and packed batch-seq-hidden indexing at a loosened 4e-4 float32 tolerance, versus the file's typical 3e-5.
An even key/value length exercises register-cached vec4 softmax on the portable materialized route with fused Q bias and post-normalization V bias.

A 512-query, 515-key attention shape with one head (head width 64) and a bias applied to Q, K and V. Key length 515 is not a multiple of four, so per-column softmax arithmetic must produce the correct result without four-wide grouping.
Head width 80, query length 520, and key/value length 516 each fall short of a round tile size, together exercising partial final tiles in the head, query, and key dimensions.
A head width of 80, query length 520, and key/value length 516 leave partial final matrix tiles; fused Q bias must not affect padded rows.
An odd KV length disables vec4 caching while preserving the generalized subgroup-matrix score/apply path; every GEMM dimension has a tail.
Two batches and head size 32 exercise the narrow-head subgroup-matrix route and the workgroup-z mapping to batch and head.

Upper-head boundary for the fused-bias f32 Q32 broadcast specialization. At two subgroup-widths of vec4 head state the clustered kernel avoids the broadcast kernel's doubled long-lived Q/output register footprint.

BSH float32 Q/K/V uses eight heads of width 64, two query tokens, and 32 keys. Rank-4 attention bias is broadcast over batch and heads; query row 1 is -Infinity at every key while row 0 is finite. The portable scalar online-attention route must return zero for every head in row 1 without forming NaN from a zero denominator; row 0 follows the ordinary softmax-weighted value calculation.

Rank-4 bias has one finite entry at key 3 and -Infinity elsewhere. The scalar softmax therefore places all mass on key 3, so every head returns value row 3. This distinguishes a valid one-key denominator from `attn_bias_scalar_all_neg_inf_row_zero_q2_kv32_h8_d64`.
Query length 30 across 270 query-head rows checks noncausal attention on subgroup and portable tiers.
Fused QKV bias with query length 30 checks bias application across query heads.
Additive attention bias with query length 30 checks output parity on tiers without subgroups.
all-MiniLM-L6-v2 self-attention at a short sentence: the whole-head small-seq variant.
A 32-token query and key/value sequence with 4 heads and head width 64 checks attention output at a short sequence length.
Cross attention: kvSeq != qSeq, and neither is a power of two (the workgroup rounds up, the tail threads must not write).
Batch > 1 drives the dispatch y axis; a wrong batch stride would mix the two sequences.
A 32-token query, key and value sequence with 12 heads and head width 32 checks attention output at a short sequence length.

Values oscillate around 1.0, keeping the attention average at order-one magnitude. This makes both the denominator published by row statistics and the division in the subgroup-matrix apply pass observable.
A 1,024-by-1,024 attention score matrix over four heads; values oscillate around 1.0 so denominator and value-scale errors remain observable.

A 1024-query, 1024-key attention shape with 4 heads (head width 64) applies separate bias vectors to Q, K and V. V values oscillate around 1.0, keeping the roughly 16 MiB score tensor's output near unit scale so a missing or misapplied bias is observable.

A monotone value ramp makes each output an order-one function of the weighted key index. This exposes both uniform scale errors and incorrect exponential offsets in the cross-partition split-K combine.
A monotone value ramp keeps float16 decode outputs at order-one magnitude, making split-K accumulation, cross-partition rescaling, and final normalization observable.
A monotone value ramp gives each float16 q32 row a distinct order-one output, exposing the register-blocked epilogue division and an incorrect broadcast lane.
A 16-query, 2,048-key attention case with a value ramp keeps outputs near unit magnitude and exposes normalization errors.
Short-sequence attention with 64 queries, 64 keys, four heads of width 16, fused bias, and causal masking.

Thirteen queries leave five active rows in the final eight-row block, and the key count is not divisible by sixteen. Causal masking makes out-of-range lanes and inactive rows contribute the identity partial.
Head dim 32 (eight vec4 per row, the route's register ceiling) with bias and no causal mask; kv > q so every query sees all forty keys.
Fewer keys than key lanes (5 keys, 8 lanes after the power-of-two floor) and fewer queries than one block: most lanes hold no key and merge identities.
Two batches of two heads at exactly two query blocks; the batch axis rides dispatch z and the bias is shared across batches.
The unmasked whole-head route always includes an `exp(0)` term, so a finite row cannot have a zero denominator. A positive-infinity query produces non-finite scores and the expected NaN result.
Peaked attention with cancellation in a 31-component score dot product; retain the dominant keys of a seeded long-context failure. Strict full-output reference checks expose score rounding errors.
